newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Russia's Luzhkov visits disputed Ukrainian port.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Luzhkov visits disputed Ukrainian port.

text.p: The powerful mayor of Moscow, in a move guaranteed to enrage Kiev, visited the Ukrainian port of Sevastopol on the Crimean peninsula on Friday and said it should be a part of Russia.
"No Russian will feel comfortable until Sevastopol is returned to the Russian Federation," Yuri Luzhkov told hundreds of people gathered by a new apartment block he was opening.
Sevastopol is populated mostly by ethnic Russians and is home to the Black Sea Fleet, whose division has led to years of bickering between former Soviet neighbours Russia and Ukraine.

Diplomatic sources in Kiev, aware that Luzhkov was planning a visit to open the 300-apartment block for Russian naval officers, have said the foreign ministry was considering declaring him persona non grata in Ukraine.

But the bald-headed mayor, widely seen as a potential candidate for a future Russian president, went ahead with the trip despite receiving a letter from Ukrainian Foreign Minister Hennady Udovenko warning him his visit would be undesirable.
Itar-Tass news agency quoted Luzhkov as writing in reply to Udovenko that he was merely exercising his right to freedom of movement in Ukraine in line with bilateral treaties.
But his previous comments that Sevastopol could even be seized by force have set him at loggerheads with Ukrainian authorities, though his view is not endorsed by the Kremlin.

"We say Sevastopol was and is a Russian city and we must defend Sevastopol's right to remain a Russian city," Luzhkov told the crowd to warm applause, though he added the port should be returned to Russia peacefully.
Udovenko was on his way back from a meeting of Commonwealth of Independent States ministers in Moscow on Friday and official reaction was not available.
But one spokesman said the foreign ministry had not expected Luzhkov to make the trip, and the reaction, when it came, would be strong.
Crimea, conquered by Russia in the 1780s, was transferred to Ukraine in 1954 under Nikita Khrushchev, at a time when the break-up of the highly centralised Soviet Union seemed unimaginable.
But Luzhkov said Sevastopol had remained a separate entity under the deal so it should have stayed a part of Russia.
"Sevastopol was never transferred to Ukraine by any document, even in Khrushchev's time, when he, in a drunken state, transferred Crimea," Luzhkov said.
Many borders between countries and regions of the former Soviet Union are disputed, as frontiers were often arbitrary and designed to separate ethnic groups or fulfil political goals.
The Kremlin ruled Ukraine for more than three centuries, but it recognised Ukrainian independence and territorial integrity at the time of the breakup of the Soviet Union in 1991.
